name: aws-l2
title: L2: schemas linked too, and shared everywhere
kicker: A preview of HEART · HEART L2
html:
L2: schemas linked too, and shared everywhere

# GET /affordance-sets/{hash}
# Prefer: forms=link, schema=link
# Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
_forms:
  clientcertificate:update:
    title: Update
    _links:
      target:
        href: /clientcertificates/{id}
        templated: true
    hr:templatePointers:
      id: /clientCertificateId
    method: PATCH
    contentType: application/json
    hr:integrity: sha256-…
    schema:
      $ref: /schemas/{hash}
      hr:integrity: sha256-…
  clientcertificate:delete:
    title: Delete
    _links:
      target:
        href: /clientcertificates/{id}
        templated: true
    hr:templatePointers:
      id: /clientCertificateId
    method: DELETE
# GET /schemas/{hash}
# Content-Type: application/schema+json
# Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
$schema: https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema
type: object
required: [patchOperations]
properties:
  patchOperations:
    type: array
    items:
      type: object
      properties:
        op:
          enum: [add, remove, replace,
                 move, copy, test]
        path:
          type: string
          examples: [/description]
        value:
          type: string
        from:
          type: string

MOCKUP Today L0 L1 L2 A second read: 304 for the certificate; set and schema from cache, no request.
say: Mockup. With Prefer: forms=link, schema=link, each form in the set references its schema by $ref, at a content address with an integrity hash. One schema, say for a patch of the description, is shared across forms, states and resources. This is the rung the release desk ran on GitHub and GitLab: from the second release on, about 50 set and schema reads per release never reached the network.

deck:ref.name: cache
deck:ref.label: Cache
deck:ref.title: Cache (§5.1.4)
deck:ref.summary: Label every response cacheable or not, so interactions can be skipped. HEART's L2 form sets are this.
deck:ref.quote:
“In order to improve network efficiency, we add cache constraints to form the client-cache-stateless-server style of Section 3.4.4 (Figure 5-4). Cache constraints require that the data within a response to a request be implicitly or explicitly labeled as cacheable or non-cacheable. If a response is cacheable, then a client cache is given the right to reuse that response data for later, equivalent requests.

The advantage of adding cache constraints is that they have the potential to partially or completely eliminate some interactions, improving efficiency, scalability, and user-perceived performance by reducing the average latency of a series of interactions. The trade-off, however, is that a cache can decrease reliability if stale data within the cache differs significantly from the data that would have been obtained had the request been sent directly to the server.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.4
